lesson.title: Sizing for the Worst Case: The Volt-Ampere
lesson.summary: The volt-ampere (VA) is the unit of apparent power, the simple product of rms voltage and rms current with no regard to phase angle, and it represents the total current-carrying burden that generators, transformers, and wiring must be sized to handle regardless of how much of that power is real or reactive.
lesson.body:
Apparent power answers a very practical question that neither real power nor reactive power answers alone: how much voltage and current does a piece of equipment actually have to be built to handle? The formula is deliberately simple, S = V x I, using rms voltage and rms current with no phase angle involved at all. That simplicity is the point. A transformer's windings do not care whether the current flowing through them is doing useful work or sloshing back and forth as reactive power, the wire heats up and the insulation stresses the same either way, purely as a function of current magnitude. So transformers, generators, and circuit breakers are rated in VA or kVA, not in watts, because VA is what determines whether the equipment survives.

Apparent power sits at the hypotenuse of the power triangle, with real power P and reactive power Q as the two legs: S^2 = P^2 + Q^2, or equivalently S = V x I directly from voltage and current magnitudes. Power factor, cos(theta) = P/S, is really just a statement of how much of that hypotenuse actually points in the useful, real-power direction.

Using the same 120 V rms, 10 A rms, 0.8 lagging power factor load from the watt and VAR discussions, the apparent power is S = V x I = 120 x 10 = 1,200 VA. Checking against the triangle relation confirms consistency with the previously computed real power of 960 W and reactive power of 720 VAR: sqrt(960^2 + 720^2) = sqrt(921,600 + 518,400) = sqrt(1,440,000) = 1,200, matching S = V x I exactly.

Apparent power ratings drive real equipment sizing decisions. Suppose a transformer is rated at 5 kVA and operates at 240 V rms. The maximum rms current it can safely deliver, regardless of the load's power factor, is I_max = S/V = 5,000 VA / 240 V = 20.83 A. If that transformer feeds a load with a poor power factor of, say, 0.6, the maximum real power it can deliver is only P = S x pf = 5,000 x 0.6 = 3,000 W, even though the transformer is fully loaded at its rated 20.83 A. Improve the load's power factor to 0.9 through power factor correction, and the same transformer, still working at the same rated current, now delivers P = 5,000 x 0.9 = 4,500 W, 1,500 W more useful power squeezed out of hardware that never changed.

That example is the clearest possible illustration of why apparent power gets its own unit distinct from the watt: two systems can draw identical volt-amperes, identical current, identical transformer stress, and yet deliver very different amounts of actual usable power depending on power factor. VA measures the burden on the equipment; watts measure the payoff for the customer.

This is also why generator and transformer nameplates almost never quote a watt rating at all, only a VA or kVA figure alongside a rated voltage: the manufacturer has no way of knowing in advance what power factor a customer's load will present, so it rates the machine by the one quantity, apparent power, that stays fixed regardless of load composition. Getting the maximum real watts out of a VA-rated machine then becomes the customer's job, achieved through power factor correction rather than through any change to the source equipment itself.
